chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Ja'far, from Al-Sayyari, from the one who mentioned it, from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I complained to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about some pain, and I said, 'The physician has prescribed a drink for me: I take raisins and pour water upon them, two parts water to one part raisins. Then I pour honey upon it, then I cook it until two-thirds of it evaporates and one-third remains.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Is it not sweet?' I said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Drink it.' (The narrator said), 'And I did not inform him how much the honey was.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on consuming a medicinal drink made of raisins, water, and honey in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the Imam’s practical approach to medicine, where the sensory quality of sweetness (hulw) serves as a sufficient indicator of permissibility for a medicinal syrup, reflecting the Shia emphasis on ease in health matters. The Imam’s inquiry about the honey quantity underscores the importance of distinguishing between medicinal use and excessive consumption that might lead to intoxication or health detriment. This narrative reinforces the principle that permissible foods retain their status when prepared for healing, provided they do not cross into prohibited categories.
